graphic-designer.intro: Learn graphic design from principles to production. Master the tools, understand client work, and build a portfolio that wins jobs — locally and remotely.

skillDomains.name: Design Fundamentals
skillDomains.description: The timeless principles that make good design, independent of software.

skills.name: Composition
skills.description: Arrange elements so the eye knows where to go.

modules.title: The four principles
modules.content:
Every good composition uses four principles:

  1. Contrast — make different things look different
  2. Alignment — put things on invisible lines
  3. Proximity — group related items together
  4. Repetition — repeat visual elements for cohesion

Before software, designers arranged type and shapes with rulers and T-squares. The principles haven't changed.

modules.title: Whitespace is a design element
modules.content:
Beginners fill every space. Professionals use empty space deliberately.

Whitespace does three things

  • Gives the eye rest
  • Creates hierarchy (empty space around something makes it important)
  • Signals quality (cheap design crowds; premium design breathes)

Rule of thumb

If you're unsure whether to add another element, don't. Nine times out of ten, less is more.

steps.q: A poster has a huge headline and tiny body text. Which principle is at work?
Three menu items are placed close together and away from other elements. Which principle?
A logo appears the same colour on the front, back, and sides of a business card. Which principle?

skills.name: Typography
skills.description: Type is 90% of design. Master it.

modules.title: Type categories
modules.content:
Serif

Has small strokes at the end of letters. Traditional, trustworthy. Example: Times, Georgia, Playfair.

Sans-serif

No strokes. Modern, clean. Example: Helvetica, Inter, Roboto.

Display

Designed for large text. Headlines only. Example: Bebas, Impact.

Script

Handwritten style. Decorative. Use sparingly.

The rule

Two fonts maximum per design. One for headlines, one for body. Three becomes chaos.

modules.title: Type hierarchy
modules.content:
Hierarchy through

  • Size — biggest text is read first
  • Weight — bold text stands out
  • Colour — high contrast draws the eye
  • Spacing — more space around something makes it prominent

The test

Squint at your design. Can you still tell what's most important? If yes, the hierarchy works. If it all looks the same, it needs contrast.

steps.q: You're designing a law firm's logo. Which type category fits best?
You have a headline, subhead, and body text. How many font families should you use?
steps.f: One or two fonts is the professional standard.

steps.q: Body text at 9pt is hard to read on mobile. What do you do?
steps.f: Body text on mobile should be 14-16pt minimum.

modules.title: Design a poster
modules.prompt: Design a poster for a local event (concert, workshop, market). Use at least two typographic sizes and clear hierarchy.
steps: Choose a real or imagined event
Sketch the layout with pen and paper first
Design in any tool (Canva, Figma, Illustrator, Photoshop)
Test by squinting — is the hierarchy clear?
Save final version and a photo of it in context

skillDomains.name: Tools
skillDomains.description: The software you'll use every day. Learn one deeply before chasing others.

skills.name: Design Software
skills.description: From Canva to Illustrator to Figma.

modules.title: Which tool for which job
modules.content:
Canva

Browser-based. Free tier. Great for quick social media, presentations, simple print. Not professional-grade for logos or complex layout.

Figma

Browser-based. Free tier. Industry standard for UI/UX and increasingly for all design. Real-time collaboration.

Adobe Illustrator

Vector design. Logos, icons, print. Industry standard for brand work.

Adobe Photoshop

Raster editing. Photos, complex composites. Not for logos or type.

The honest advice

Learn Figma first (free, versatile). Add Illustrator when you get brand work. Skip Canva for anything paid — it looks like Canva.

steps.q: A client needs a logo that scales from business card to billboard. Which tool?
You need to remove a background from a photo. Which tool?
steps.f: Photoshop is the raster editing tool.

skillDomains.name: Client Work
skillDomains.description: Turn design skill into income. Managing clients is a discipline of its own.

skills.name: Briefing
skills.description: Understand what the client actually needs before you design.

modules.title: Why briefs matter
modules.content:
A vague brief leads to revisions and lost money. Every design project should start with a written brief covering:

  • What is being designed (logo, poster, app screen)
  • Who is the audience
  • Where will it appear (print, screen, both)
  • What tone — playful, serious, premium, cheap
  • What's the budget and timeline
  • What does success look like

Get the brief in writing before starting. It protects both sides.

modules.title: Revisions — how to control them
modules.content:
Unlimited revisions destroy profit. A design that gets revised 20 times takes 20 times longer and pays the same.

The fix

  • Include a set number of revisions in the price (2-3 is standard)
  • Charge for additional rounds
  • Present two or three options — not ten
  • Ask for all feedback in one round, not piecemeal

This isn't being difficult. It's how professional design businesses survive.

modules.title: Design a complete brand identity
modules.prompt: Choose a real or imagined business. Design a complete brand identity: logo, colour palette, typography, and 3 example applications (business card, social post, signage).
